The reproduction works. With `buf[8]` and a 4-byte UTF-8 sequence encoding U+1F4A9, it writes 7 bytes (`\u1f4a9`). Now let me test with a smaller buffer to trigger the overflow. Let me use `buf[7]` so that `available = 7`, and the write of 7 bytes overflows by... wait, `available - written = 7 >= 6`, so it proceeds, then writes 7 bytes into a 7-byte buffer. That's exactly at the boundary (no overflow). Let me use `buf[6]` — then `available - written = 6 >= 6`, proceeds, writes 7 bytes into a 6-byte buffer → 1-byte overflow!

Wait, but the check at the top is `if (available <= required) return FLB_FALSE;`. With `buf[6]`, `available = 6`, `required = 4`. `6 <= 4`? No. So proceed. Then in the loop, `available - written = 6 < 2`? No. `c = 0xF0` (signed char = -16, so `c = 0xFFFFFFF0 > 0xFFFF`). Enter `c > 0xFFFF` branch. `hex_bytes = flb_utf8_len(str+0)`. For 0xF0, `trailingBytesForUTF8[0xF0] = 3`, so `hex_bytes = 4`. Check `available - written < 6`? `6 < 6`? No. Proceed. Check `i + hex_bytes > str_len`? `0 + 4 > 4`? No. Decode. codepoint = 0x1F4A9. `len = snprintf(tmp, 15, "\\u%04x", 0x1F4A9)` = 7. `encoded_to_buf(p, tmp, 7)` writes 7 bytes into a buffer with only 6 bytes available → 1-byte overflow!

Let me test this.
